title: upperstory/spintronics-simulator
note: The checkout loads Phaser and Planck.js and represents chains with radius- and wrap-dependent gear constraints (ref/spintronics-simulator/public/index.html:94 and ref/spintronics-simulator/public/part-manager.js:318). Under ref/spintronics-simulator/public/parts/, resistor damping and density scale with R (resistor-part.js:177), inductor density scales with L (inductor-part.js:153), capacitor restoring torque scales with −angle/C (capacitor-part.js:224), the motor applies constant torque while driving (motor-part.js:280), and the sprung transistor gate sets channel damping to max(0.5, 100^(2(1−r)) − 1) for clamped gate travel r (transistor-part.js:273 and transistor-part.js:283).

title: A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, Vol. II
note: In §604 Maxwell treats currents as velocities in a dynamical account of coupled circuits. The passage shows the historical current–velocity correspondence behind the impedance analogy.

title: An introduction to energy harvesting and micro-power management
note: The slide on equivalent electromechanical circuits represents the same mass–spring–damper with a Maxwell series RLC circuit and a Firestone parallel circuit. It shows how the choice of analogy affects circuit topology.

title: Bond Graphs: A Unifying Framework for Modelling of Physical Systems
note: The impedance analogy pairs force or torque with voltage and linear or angular velocity with current. Applying Broenink’s mapping to Upper Story’s science guide puts Spintronics in the impedance analogy because differential chain tension supplies the force and chain travel per unit time supplies the velocity.

title: Analysis and Design of Engineering Systems
note: Paynter’s MIT course notes develop bond graphs from power exchange through paired effort and flow variables. An ideal 0-junction shares effort and balances signed flows, like KCL, and a 1-junction shares flow and balances signed efforts, like KVL.

title: Spintronic Junction Value Pack
note: The planetary differential enforces v_bottom = v_middle + v_top for the signed tangential speeds of the sprocket teeth. With chain speed mapped to current, that is Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL) at the junction.

title: Spintronic Inductor (55 H)
note: Upper Story describes momentum storage in a rotor with peripheral steel balls. The simulator pivots the rotor against a fixed frame (ref/spintronics-simulator/public/parts/inductor-part.js:64), so its flywheel is a grounded rotational inertia, the fixed-terminal case of Smith’s two-terminal inerter.

title: The Inerter: A Retrospective
note: Distinguishes the ideal inerter from hardware implementations and discusses the rotational form, where torque is proportional to relative angular acceleration between two terminals.

title: Synthesis of electrical and mechanical networks of restricted complexity
note: Section 3.5 compares the impedance analogy with Firestone’s 1933 mobility analogy, detailed in the Papers section. In the topology-preserving mobility mapping, nodal force balance corresponds to KCL and the signed sum of relative velocities around a closed mechanical loop corresponds to KVL.

title: The Hydraulic Analogues of Basic Circuits: Labs for Online Learning Environments
note: Uses hydraulic circuits to demonstrate Ohm’s law and RC charging. Flow rate serves as current and pressure difference as voltage, giving another physical analogue for the same circuit laws.

title: Turing Tumble – Build Marble-Powered Computers
note: Upper Story’s marble-powered logic kit uses mechanical computers to solve puzzles. It provides a comparison with the chain-based circuit kit from the same maker.

title: Turing Tumble: Gaming on a Mechanical Computer
note: The early campaign updates document Turing Tumble’s crowdfunding and describe its underlying marble-computer puzzle format.

title: Turing Tumble Simulator (ttsim)
note: A browser simulator for the marble kit. It provides a software comparison with the Spintronics simulator.

title: DIGI-COMP 1 model 101 (Educational)
note: The collection record describes a plastic kit programmed by relocating logic tubes to perform binary arithmetic and other operations. The year refers to the object.

title: Digi-Comp II
note: The museum describes Godfrey’s marble-driven binary kit, where mechanical switches and flip-flops route the balls to perform arithmetic. The year refers to the design in the record.

title: Manchester University Differential Analyser
note: The collection records a machine built for solving differential equations with interconnected mechanical integrators, following Douglas Hartree’s Meccano model. The year refers to the instrument’s completion.

title: William Thomson’s Tide Predicting Machine, 1872
note: Describes Kelvin’s geared shafts, cranks, and pulleys for representing tidal constituents and tracing their combined curve. The year refers to the instrument.

title: Tide-Predicting Machine No. 2
note: NOAA documents an instrument that mechanically summed 37 tidal constituents and traced a prediction curve. The year refers to the instrument’s completion.

title: The Mechanical Analog Computers of Hannibal Ford and William Newell
note: This historical account traces naval fire-control computers as an application of continuous mechanical computation, from early range keepers through the Second World War.

title: Mechanical Logic Gates With Amplification
note: Reports on capstan lever logic, where a powered pulley supplies output gain. The linked project demonstrates an inverter, half adder, and RS flip-flop.

title: A New Analogy Between Mechanical and Electrical Systems
note: Firestone’s mobility analogy maps force to current and velocity to voltage. In this mapping the mechanical network topology is preserved, and mass and spring compliance correspond to capacitance and inductance, respectively.

title: Synthesis of Mechanical Networks: The Inerter
note: Defines a two-terminal element whose terminal force is proportional to relative acceleration, removing the fixed-terminal restriction of a lumped mass. Smith uses the mobility analogy for synthesis, so the ideal inerter plays the role of a capacitor in that mapping.

title: The Differential Analyzer. A New Machine for Solving Differential Equations
note: Bush describes how reconfigurable shaft connections, mechanical integrators, and torque amplifiers solve ordinary differential equations.

title: Circuit-Based Design of Microfluidic Drop Networks
note: The hydraulic analogy maps pressure difference to voltage and volumetric flow rate to current. The paper applies it to channel resistance and extends the circuit model to nonlinear hanging and standing drops.

title: Turing Tumble is Turing-Complete
note: Proves universality by simulating a Turing machine on a hypothetical infinitely long board with unlimited pieces. The proof makes explicit which idealisations extend the physical kit.

title: The Design Principles of Konrad Zuse’s Mechanical Computers
note: Describes the mechanical relays and interconnections of Zuse’s programmable binary Z1. It is an example of digital logic built from plates and rods.

title: Mechanical transistors for logic-with-memory computing
note: Uses temperature signals and a bistable mechanical actuator to combine logic and memory. It provides a comparison with Spintronics’ spring-return gate, which controls channel damping.

title: Cascading of Nanomechanical Resonator Logic
note: Models two cascaded nanomechanical NAND gates and identifies a timing constraint on transmitting the output downstream. It analyzes signal transfer between mechanical logic stages at a different scale from capstan or chain logic.
